A Facebook Love Story Inspired by an OFW in Hong Kong

sections.title: Preface
sections.html:
Preface

Some stories begin with fireworks. This one begins with a notification.

Last Seen Online is a story about connection in the digital age--about how small messages, kind questions, and ordinary conversations can become lifelines. It is inspired by the lives of many people who work far from home, especially OFWs who carry family, responsibility, and loneliness with quiet strength.

This book is not about one person saving another. It is about noticing. It is about kindness. It is about asking people not only how they are, but how they are really doing.

sections.title: Chapter 1
sections.html:
Chapter 1

Last Seen: 11:47 PM

By the time Lia Santos reached the tiny room she shared with two other women in Hong Kong, the city was still wide awake.

Outside the window, neon lights blinked against the glass like restless stars. Buses hissed below. People hurried along the sidewalk with shopping bags, phones, and places to go. Somewhere nearby, someone laughed too loudly, and somewhere farther away, the soft wail of an ambulance disappeared between the tall buildings.

Hong Kong never seemed to sleep.

But Lia was tired enough for the whole city.

She slipped off her white rubber shoes by the door and leaned one hand against the wall. Her feet ached from standing all day. Her back carried the kind of pain that did not shout but stayed quietly, like an old debt. She closed her eyes for a moment and breathed in the familiar smell of their room--laundry soap, instant coffee, dried fish from someone's dinner, and the faint perfume Ate Grace sprayed every morning before work.

"Late ka na naman," Ate Grace said from the lower bunk, not looking up from her phone.

Lia forced a smile. "Madam had visitors."

"Visitors means extra work."

"Always."

Ate Grace clicked her tongue. "Eat first."

"I'm not hungry."

"That means you're very hungry."

Lia laughed softly, but it came out more like a sigh. She placed her bag on the plastic chair near her bed and pulled out her phone charger. Her battery was at six percent. Just like her energy, she thought.

Six percent and still expected to function.

She changed into an old oversized T-shirt and sat on the edge of her narrow mattress. The room was small, but it held many dreams. On one side, Ate Grace had taped pictures of her children in Iloilo. On the other, their other roommate, Mel, had taped a calendar with red circles around salary days. Lia's own corner had only two things: a small rosary hanging from a nail and a picture of her mother in the Philippines, smiling beside a pot of bougainvillea.

Every month, Lia sent most of her salary home.

For Nanay's medicine.

For her younger brother's tuition.

For the leaking roof that always needed "one more repair."

For emergencies that arrived more faithfully than blessings.

She did not complain. At least not out loud. That was the first rule of being strong: people praised your strength only when you carried pain quietly.

Her phone buzzed as soon as she plugged it in.

A message from Nanay.

Nanay: Anak, kumain ka na?

Nanay: Salamat sa pinadala mo. Nakabili na ako gamot.

Nanay: Ingat ka palagi diyan.

Lia stared at the screen until the words blurred a little.

She typed back:

Lia: Opo Nay. Kumain na ako. Love you. Matulog na kayo.

It was a lie.

She had not eaten.

But sometimes love sounded like lies when you did not want someone to worry.

She put the phone down and reached for the plastic container Ate Grace had left on the table. Rice. Egg. A few pieces of sausage. Simple food. Good enough. She ate slowly while scrolling through Facebook with one thumb.

Facebook was her little window to everyone else's life.

A cousin posted a beach trip.

A former classmate posted a new car.

An auntie shared a quote about fake friends.

Someone from her hometown posted a blurry karaoke video.

Lia smiled at some, ignored most, and kept scrolling. At night, after work, Facebook made her feel close to home and far from it at the same time. It reminded her that life was continuing without her in places she still loved.

Then one post made her thumb stop.

It was not from a friend.

Maybe someone had shared it. Maybe the algorithm had carried it to her, the way the sea carried bottles to strangers.

The post had no picture. Just a plain dark background with white words:

People think silence means peace.
Sometimes silence means someone is tired of explaining pain nobody understands.

Lia read it once.

Then again.

The words sat heavily in her chest.

She did not know the man who posted it. His name was Daniel Reyes. His profile picture was simple: a man standing near what looked like a lake, wearing a dark jacket, his face half-turned away from the camera. He did not look like someone trying to impress anyone. No flashy smile. No expensive watch. No dramatic pose.

Just a man looking somewhere far away.

Lia tapped his name.

His profile loaded slowly.

Lives in Texas.

Originally from the Philippines.

A few public posts. Mostly quotes. Some photos of coffee, sunsets, quiet roads, and once, a picture of an empty chair beside a window.

There was sadness in his page, but not the kind that begged for attention. It was the kind that hid in ordinary things.

Lia looked back at the post.

Her finger hovered over the reactions.

Like?

Care?

Heart?

She did not know why it mattered. He was a stranger. A stranger in Texas, thousands of miles away from her small room in Hong Kong. He would probably never notice one reaction from a woman he did not know.

Still, the words felt too honest to pass without answering.

So Lia pressed the heart.

A small red symbol appeared under his post.

Then she locked her phone and placed it beside her pillow.

"Matulog ka na," Ate Grace said. "Tomorrow again."

"Tomorrow again," Lia repeated.

She lay down and pulled the thin blanket over herself. Above her, the bunk bed creaked as Mel shifted in her sleep. Outside, Hong Kong continued glowing, moving, wanting, rushing.

Lia closed her eyes.

But the post stayed with her.

Sometimes silence means someone is tired of explaining pain nobody understands.

She knew that kind of silence.

She knew what it meant to smile on video calls so her mother would not hear exhaustion in her voice. She knew what it meant to type "I'm okay" when she was not okay. She knew what it meant to carry everyone's needs while quietly forgetting her own.

Her phone buzzed again.

She opened one eye.

Probably Nanay again. Or a group chat. Or Facebook reminding her of something useless.

But the notification was different.

Daniel Reyes liked your reaction.

Lia blinked.

Then another notification appeared.

Daniel Reyes sent you a message request.

For a moment, she only stared.

The room was dim except for the glow of her phone. Ate Grace was still scrolling. Mel was still asleep. The city outside was still awake.

Lia tapped the message.

There was only one sentence.

Daniel Reyes: Thank you for the heart. I didn't think anyone would understand that post.

Lia read it twice.

Then she looked at the time.

11:47 PM.

She should sleep. She had work early. She had responsibilities waiting before sunrise. She had no business replying to a stranger from Texas who wrote sad quotes on Facebook.

But something about the message felt gentle.

Not flirtatious.

Not demanding.

Just lonely.

Lia placed her thumb on the keyboard.

She thought for a moment.

Then she typed:

Lia Santos: Maybe I understood it because I feel that way too sometimes.

She stared at the words before sending them.

It felt too honest.

Too personal.

Too much for a stranger.

But maybe that was why it felt safe.

She pressed send.

A second later, three moving dots appeared.

Daniel was typing.

Lia's heart gave a small, unexpected jump.

Outside her window, Hong Kong shimmered like a thousand lives she would never enter.

Inside her phone, someone on the other side of the world was awake.

And for the first time in a long time, Lia did not feel completely invisible.

sections.title: Chapter 2
sections.html:
Chapter 2

One Notification

Texas was quiet in a different way.

Not silent.

Just... slower.

Daniel Reyes stood by the kitchen counter holding a mug of coffee that had already gone cold. Morning sunlight stretched across the floor in pale rectangles, and somewhere outside, a lawn mower hummed in the distance.

He had been awake since five.

Not because he wanted to.

His body simply forgot how to sleep properly.

He picked up his phone and unlocked it.

No new messages.

No missed calls.

A few Facebook notifications.

Normally he ignored them. Most were random things anyway--suggested pages, old memories, someone changing profile pictures.

But one notification stayed at the top.

Lia Santos reacted with a heart to your post.

Daniel stared at it.

He almost cleared it.

Instead, he tapped.

Her profile opened. Her display photo showed a woman sitting near a waterfront at sunset. She wasn't posing dramatically. No heavy filters. Just a simple smile and eyes that looked tired and kind at the same time.

Her profile wasn't public enough to tell much.

Lives in Hong Kong.

From the Philippines.

A few travel photos. Food. Shared quotes. Nothing unusual.

But she didn't look like someone who reacted randomly.

Daniel looked back at the post. That post. He almost deleted it last night.

He had typed it without thinking. Actually, not typed. Released. Sometimes thoughts sat inside him too long and escaped as short sentences online.

Usually people reacted with thumbs-up. They rarely understood.

But she reacted with a heart.

That felt different.

Not agreement. Recognition.

Daniel placed his coffee down and opened Messenger. He paused, closed it, opened it again.

This is stupid.

He was not someone who messaged strangers. He disliked awkward conversations. And honestly, people disappeared anyway.

Still, he typed:

Thank you for the heart. I didn't think anyone would understand that post.

He stared at the message. Deleted it. Typed again. Deleted again. Finally he sent it.

Immediately regretted it.

Great. Now she'll think I'm weird.

Daniel put the phone face down and walked toward the window. Outside, the neighborhood looked ordinary. Cars. Trees. People living normal lives. He wondered when normal stopped feeling normal.

His phone vibrated.

Message Request Accepted.

Daniel blinked.

Then read:

Maybe I understood it because I feel that way too sometimes.

He read it again.

No emoji. No performance. No "haha." Just honest.

His chest tightened unexpectedly.

He sat down.

What do you even say to that?

I’m sorry you feel that way too, he typed.

Three dots appeared. Stopped. Appeared again.

Don't be sorry. Maybe people like us are just tired.

People like us.

Strange phrase.

But it felt familiar.

Long day? he asked.

Very long. I just got home from work.

Night shift?

No. Long shift. Hong Kong doesn't stop.

Daniel smiled faintly. First smile today.

Texas is slower, he typed.

Must be nice.

Daniel looked around his apartment. Cold coffee. Unwashed mug. Quiet rooms. The TV he never turned on.

Sometimes too quiet.

Seen.

No reply.

Thirty seconds. One minute. Two.

Daniel locked the phone. Too much. Too serious. See? This is why you don't message strangers.

He started washing dishes.

Phone buzzed.

Quiet sounds nice until you have nobody to talk to.

Daniel stopped moving. Water continued running. He turned it off.

That might be the most honest thing I've read this week.

Sleep first, she replied. We can continue this conversation some other time.

Daniel stared. Simple. No pressure. No pretending.

Good night, Hong Kong.

A few seconds later, a heart reaction appeared on his message.

Daniel put his phone down.

For the first time in weeks, the apartment did not feel as empty.

And in a small room across the world, someone probably smiled too.

He looked once more at the message thread.

One reaction.

One notification.

Nothing important.

At least, that was what he told himself.

sections.title: Chapter 3
sections.html:
Chapter 3

Messenger Request

The next morning, Lia woke up before her alarm.

That almost never happened. Usually, her body fought every minute of sleep like it was treasure.

But today she opened her eyes at 5:22 AM.

For a second she didn't know why.

Then she remembered.

Messenger.

Her phone was charging beside her pillow. She reached for it.

No new message.

She stared at the screen a little longer than necessary.

Then laughed quietly at herself.

What exactly was she expecting? That a stranger in Texas would suddenly send her a morning greeting? Ridiculous.

She sat up. The room was still dim. Ate Grace was asleep. Mel had already left for work.

Lia stretched and started getting ready. Hair tied. Simple makeup. Work clothes. Coffee. Normal morning.

But while waiting for the kettle to boil, she opened Facebook.

No notification.

She closed it. Opened Messenger. Still nothing.

Okay. Enough. Back to real life.

She grabbed her bag and headed downstairs. Hong Kong greeted her the way it always did--fast. People moving. Phones ringing. Crosswalk sounds. The smell of bakery bread mixing with traffic.

She got on the train and found a spot near the door. Her reflection in the window looked tired.

She opened her phone again.

Still no message.

Why do I care?

She locked the screen.

Two seconds later--buzz.

Her heart reacted before her brain.

Messenger.

Daniel Reyes.

Good morning. Or... good evening? I forgot the time difference already.

Lia smiled before she realized she was smiling.

Good evening for you. Good morning for me, she replied.

See? I already failed geography.

Texas is not geography. It's survival.

Okay, that was unexpectedly funny.

Lia laughed softly, and a woman beside her looked over.

Her train arrived. She got off and walked toward work.

Big work day? Daniel asked.

Same as yesterday. And tomorrow.

Then work swallowed her whole.

Hours passed. Laundry. Cleaning. Cooking. Helping. Carrying. Smiling.

By lunch she forgot about Messenger.

Until break time.

She sat alone with packed rice and chicken and opened her phone.

Three messages.

Question.

What's the best Filipino comfort food?

This is important research.

Lia smiled.

Depends how sad you are.

That's concerning.

Mild sadness = pancit. Heartbreak = adobo. Life crisis = unlimited rice.

America doesn't have this emotional food classification.

Now you know. Filipino science.

Then Daniel asked what she did when work got too heavy.

She stared at the question.

I tell myself I'm doing it for someone.

That’s a good answer, he replied. I think I forgot how to do that.

Maybe you don't need to figure out forever today. Maybe just tomorrow.

A pause.

You know... you're easy to talk to.

Maybe because we're strangers.

Maybe, Daniel wrote. Or maybe strangers tell the truth because there's nothing to lose.

The sentence followed her back to work.

That evening on the train, Lia opened Messenger again.

Too late. Already skipped lunch.

But I had coffee. That counts.

Also... thanks for talking today.

Good. Talk tomorrow, she typed.

Tomorrow sounds nice.

Such a normal sentence.

Yet for some reason, it felt warmer than it should.

Outside, Hong Kong rushed by. Inside her pocket, someone in Texas had become part of her day.

And neither of them noticed it happening.

sections.title: Chapter 4
sections.html:
Chapter 4

Time Zones

Three days later, Lia realized she had developed a habit.

Not a big habit. Not dramatic. Just small enough to deny.

Every morning before getting out of bed, she checked Messenger. Not because she expected anything. Not because she cared. Definitely not because she wanted to see if someone from Texas had messaged.

Just checking. That was all.

This morning there was one unread message.

Good evening, Hong Kong.

Lia smiled immediately, then frowned at herself.

Good morning, Texas.

See? I still fail time zones.

At least you're consistent.

Coffee?

She looked at the small instant coffee packet in her hand and sent a picture of her plain mug.

Luxury edition.

Seconds later, Daniel sent a photo of black coffee.

Depression coffee.

Lia laughed out loud. Ate Grace looked over.

"Anong nakakatawa?"

"Wala."

On the train, Daniel asked: What's one thing nobody knows about you?

Lia typed, deleted, typed again.

I cry in the shower sometimes so nobody notices.

The answer made him quiet.

That answer makes me sad, he wrote. Mine? People think I'm quiet because I'm calm. Actually I'm quiet because I don't always have energy to explain how I feel.

That sounds exhausting.

It is.

Then came another question. What makes you happy lately?

Video calls with my family. Salary day. Sleep. Good food.

Then she added: And unexpectedly... talking to strangers.

Unexpectedly... same.

Throughout the day, the messages appeared like small lights.

Update: I ate lunch.

Congratulations.

This level of support changed my life.

Charge your phone.

Who told you it's dying?

You reply slower.

That’s scary. You noticed.

That night, Daniel asked if it felt strange that they talked every day.

A little, Lia admitted.

Same, he replied. But not bad strange.

Maybe because we don't know each other but somehow understand each other.

You know what's funny? You're twelve hours ahead. But somehow I look forward to your replies.

Lia read the sentence three times.

Sleep, Texas.

Good night, Hong Kong.

Talk tomorrow?

Tomorrow.

Outside, Hong Kong remained awake. Inside, for the first time in a long time, tomorrow felt like something to look forward to.

sections.title: Chapter 5
sections.html:
Chapter 5

Seen

Nobody warned Lia that routines could become important.

Especially small ones. The dangerous kind. The kind that looked harmless.

Like checking Messenger while waiting for coffee. Like smiling when a notification appeared. Like expecting someone's message before sleeping.

For almost two weeks, Daniel had become part of her day.

This morning, she woke to one unread message.

Good morning. Don't skip breakfast.

Only if you promise lunch.

Seen.

No reply.

That was normal. He was probably busy.

Work. Train. Routine.

An hour later, nothing. Lunch, still nothing. By afternoon, the tiny word looked louder.

Seen.

Ate Grace noticed. "You waiting for salary?"

"No."

"Boy?"

"Stranger," Lia answered before she could stop herself.

Ate Grace grinned. "Stranger? Ay wow. Online era na talaga."

"It's not like that."

And it wasn't. Was it?

That evening, Lia opened Facebook and saw Daniel had posted three hours earlier.

Some days I don't know what version of me people are talking to.

Something felt off.

She opened Messenger.

Hey. Everything okay?

Seen.

No reply.

Thirty minutes later: Sorry. Rough day.

Do you want to talk?

Not today.

Okay. I hope tomorrow feels lighter.

Seen.

No reply.

That night, after she turned off the light, her phone buzzed.

Thank you for not forcing me to explain.

Good night, Hong Kong.

Good night, Texas.

Seen.

Nothing after.

And for the first time, Lia realized she missed someone who had not actually gone anywhere.

sections.title: Chapter 6
sections.html:
Chapter 6

Daily Habit

The next morning, there was no message.

Lia told herself she didn't notice. She woke up, made coffee, got dressed, checked Messenger. Nothing.

Normal. People have lives.

On the train, her phone buzzed.

Good evening. Sorry about yesterday.

Another message: I disappeared a little.

You don't have to apologize. Everybody disappears sometimes.

You sound like someone who understands that too well.

Maybe.

Can I ask something?

Go.

When you're having a hard day... who do you talk to?

She stared.

Usually nobody.

Same.

Then he added: Actually that's not true anymore. Now apparently I send coffee updates to someone in Hong Kong.

Lia laughed in public.

The day felt lighter. Not because work changed, but because something small kept showing up.

Photo: coffee.

Caption: Lunch. Keeping promises.

Photo: rice.

Caption: Proud of you.

That felt aggressive, he wrote.

That night, he admitted he had started timing his replies so they arrived before she slept.

That's unnecessary, she wrote.

Maybe. But I think I like knowing someone will read it.

Her room was ordinary. Ate Grace watched videos. Mel folded clothes.

But inside Lia, something shifted.

Sleep, Texas.

Good night, Hong Kong.

Talk tomorrow?

Tomorrow.

She closed her eyes and realized it wasn't the messages anymore. It was the expectation.

The quiet certainty that somewhere, twelve hours away, someone would say good morning.

And somehow, that had started feeling like home.

sections.title: Chapter 7
sections.html:
Chapter 7

Stories We Don’t Post

The conversation changed so gradually neither of them noticed when it happened.

There was no sudden confession. No moment where somebody said, Tell me everything.

It just shifted.

Questions became longer. Replies became slower. Not because interest disappeared, but because answers started meaning something.

That evening, Daniel asked: What's something people think about you that isn't true?

People think I'm strong, Lia typed. But I think I just got used to carrying things.

That's a heavy answer.

Your turn.

People think I'm okay because I function. But functioning and being okay are not always the same thing.

That sentence sounds practiced.

Maybe because I've been saying "I'm fine" for a long time.

Do people know?

No. I got good at looking normal.

When I video call my family, Lia admitted, I smile more than I feel.

Why?

Because I work far away. If I look tired they feel guilty. And if I complain they worry. So I mostly say everything is okay.

That sounds lonely.

I think being OFW means becoming professionally okay.

Daniel wrote: People think sadness always looks dramatic. Sometimes it just looks like not answering texts. Or losing interest in things you used to love. Or feeling tired even after sleeping.

That sounds hard.

It is. But talking has helped.

Good.

Then he asked: What’s one thing you wish someone asked you more often?

Lia looked at the question for a long time.

If I'm okay.

Are you okay?

No one asked like that. Not really.

Today? A little tired. But okay.

Your turn. Are you okay?

Today? A little better.

They weren’t fixing each other. They weren’t rescuing each other. They were just showing up.

And sometimes, that was enough.

sections.title: Chapter 8
sections.html:
Chapter 8

Profile Pictures

It happened on a Wednesday.

Lia woke up late, missed her usual train, burned her toast, forgot her umbrella. By lunch she was convinced the universe had chosen her specifically for inconvenience.

Then Messenger notified her: Daniel Reyes updated his profile picture.

She tapped.

Daniel sat outside a cafe, coffee in one hand, dark shirt, slight smile. Nothing dramatic. But different. Lighter.

His eyes looked less tired.

Wait. That coffee cup.

The small printed text read: Try new places.

A week ago, she had told him to try somewhere new.

Coincidence. Right?

Did you see my profile picture? Daniel asked.

Maybe.

Honest opinion?

You look less tired.

Long pause.

That's interesting. Nobody said that. Nice shirt, nice background, nice coffee. You noticed something else.

Maybe because I know your old face.

Lia stared in horror after sending it.

But Daniel replied: I think that's the nicest thing someone said to me this month.

She asked why he didn't post himself often.

I stopped liking photos of myself. At some point I stopped recognizing myself.

Well, Lia wrote, I think this one looks like someone trying.

He reacted with a heart.

Then he challenged her to update her own profile picture. She refused, then later, at the waterfront after work, she updated a simple photo of herself smiling.

Thirty seconds later: Okay wow.

You look happy in that picture.

I was.

You should let people see that version of you more often.

For the first time, someone had noticed her. Not the profile. Not the smile.

Her.

And she wasn't sure what to do with that.

sections.title: Chapter 9
sections.html:
Chapter 9

The Video Call

Lia did not mean to call him.

That part was important.

It started with coffee. Daniel sent a picture: Research update: tried another cafe. Disappointing.

Lia replied with instant coffee: Professional opinion: mine looks sad but tastes loyal.

Then Daniel asked whether people acted differently online.

Sometimes online is where people tell the truth, Lia wrote.

Want to test the theory?

Meaning?

Video call. Five minutes.

No.

Because people who live in my phone should stay in my phone.

He laughed with an emoji and then, without warning, a video call request appeared.

DECLINE.

Okay wow rejected internationally.

You surprised me!

One minute. No pressure.

She stared at herself: messy hair, oversized shirt, tired eyes. No makeup. No preparation.

Five minutes later, she pressed call.

Connecting.

Ring.

Click.

And suddenly Texas existed.

Daniel appeared, blinked, and said, "Oh."

"What does that mean?" Lia asked.

"No, no--not bad. This is weird."

"Very."

They laughed. That made it easier.

He saw Hong Kong through her window. She saw his quiet kitchen in Texas. He said she laughed more than he expected. She told him he talked more than she expected.

Conversation became easier. Weather. Food. Trains. Bad coffee.

At one point he said, "This sounds weird, but it's nice to know you're real."

"Same," she answered.

Then he checked the time.

"It's been forty minutes."

"What?" she said.

He laughed. "You said one minute."

Before she ended, he said, "Thanks for calling."

"Good night, Texas."

"Good morning, Hong Kong."

Call ended.

Messenger buzzed later.

You looked exactly how I imagined. Actually... happier.

Messages made people familiar.

But hearing someone laugh made them harder to ignore.

sections.title: Chapter 10
sections.html:
Chapter 10

Offline

The day after the video call, everything felt normal.

Which somehow made it worse.

Lia could now imagine Daniel's voice when she read his messages: the pauses, the quiet laugh, the smile before the words.

By lunch, he asked where she would go if she could wake up anywhere tomorrow.

Home, she replied immediately.

Your turn.

I don't know anymore.

That's illegal. Pick somewhere.

Maybe somewhere quiet. No expectations.

That sounds less like a place and more like rest.

He reacted with a heart.

Then he went quiet.

No lunch update. No coffee photo. No random question.

By evening his last active status said eight hours ago.

She told herself not to worry.

At 10:04 PM, a message arrived: Sorry. Long day.

You okay?

Yeah. Just tired.

Sleep early.

Good night, Hong Kong.

Good night, Texas.

The next morning, no message.

Second day, no message.

Third day, no message.

No posts. No active status. Nothing.

She typed and deleted so many messages before finally sending: No pressure. Just checking in.

Delivered.

Nothing.

That night, Ate Grace asked if she missed something.

"I don't miss anybody," Lia said.

Her phone buzzed.

Daniel.

Need a little time.

I'll explain later.

Lia typed only one sentence.

Okay. I'll be here.

Seen.

No reply.

And suddenly she understood: she had started leaving emotional space for someone.

And now it was empty.

sections.title: Chapter 11
sections.html:
Chapter 11

Delivered

The first day felt understandable.

The second day felt unusual.

By the fifth day, silence started becoming a thing.

Lia acted normal. Worked. Smiled. Called home. Sent money. Watched videos. Laughed when appropriate.

And checked Messenger too often.

Every morning: Delivered.

Every lunch break: Delivered.

Before sleeping: Delivered.

No Seen. No active status. Nothing.

Ate Grace finally sat beside her and asked, "Still no reply?"

"What?"

"You're checking your phone every six minutes."

"I am not."

"Okay. Every seven."

Then softer: "Did something happen?"

"Nothing. We just talked a lot."

Ate Grace nodded. "That's enough. People don't have to be official to matter."

That night, Lia opened Messenger. The last message still said delivered.

Then, suddenly, the tiny gray word changed.

Seen.

Her heart stopped.

No typing. No message.

She typed: Hey.

Seen.

Nothing.

Then typing appeared, stopped, appeared again.

Sorry.

You don't have to apologize.

I disappeared.

You said you needed time.

I know. I didn't mean for it to become this long.

Are you okay?

Honestly? Not really. But I don't know how to explain yet.

Okay, Lia typed. You don't owe me explanations. I just wanted to know you were still there.

I didn't know someone would notice I disappeared.

I noticed.

Thank you.

A minute later, Active Now disappeared.

Offline.

Lia didn't feel relieved exactly. But she knew whatever he wasn't saying was bigger than she thought.

sections.title: Chapter 12
sections.html:
Chapter 12

Searching

After that night, Daniel disappeared again.

Not completely. This time there were signs. Messages became shorter. Replies arrived hours later. Sometimes one sentence. Sometimes none.

No more coffee updates. No random questions. No jokes.

Just small signs of someone present but far away.

One evening, Lia opened his Facebook profile and scrolled through old posts.

You can disappear slowly and people will still call you okay because you showed up to work.

Being tired is easy to explain. Being empty isn't.

The words felt less like quotes now. More like records.

During dinner, Ate Grace asked, "Do you miss him?"

"No," Lia answered too fast.

Then softer: "I think I miss... talking."

"Same thing sometimes," Ate Grace said.

That night, Lia sent: Question of the day.

Seen.

Nothing.

Then: That feels familiar.

Trying your method.

Dangerous. Soon you'll ask strangers difficult questions.

What do you do on hard days?

Usually? Wait for them to pass.

Does that work?

Not really.

What helps?

Distraction. Work. Sleep. Pretending.

Anything else?

Lately? Talking.

Good.

Then he asked why she kept messaging.

Because you said you'd explain later.

That's not the whole reason.

Maybe because I didn't want you to think nobody noticed.

Nobody usually does.

Well. I noticed.

I know. That scared me a little.

Why?

Because I realized I started expecting you too.

Lia stared.

Suddenly, she wasn't the only one who noticed the silence.

sections.title: Chapter 13
sections.html:
Chapter 13

The Truth

After that message, Lia didn't reply immediately.

Not because she didn't know what to say. Because she knew exactly what not to say.

Don't make it bigger. Don't assume. Don't rush.

You don't have to answer if you don't want to, she finally typed. But I'm here.

The next day, Daniel sent a message.

Can I tell you something and you promise not to make it a bigger deal than it is?

I can try.

Last month I stopped answering almost everybody. Family. Friends. Group chats. Not because I was angry. I just didn't have energy.

I'd wake up tired. Go to work. Come home. Sleep. Repeat.

Then people ask what's wrong and I don't know how to answer because technically nothing is wrong.

You ever feel guilty because your life is okay but you still feel bad?

Lia read that twice.

I think people feel that more than they admit.

Then the messages pile up, Daniel wrote. Then you avoid them because answering feels overwhelming. Then people stop checking.

Is that why you disappeared?

Partly. And partly because talking to you became important. Which sounds ridiculous because we barely know each other. And that scared me.

Why?

Because I started looking forward to your messages. Then one day I realized if you stopped replying I'd notice. And suddenly I cared.

That doesn't sound ridiculous, Lia replied. I think routines become important because they show up consistently. And people don't always realize they're important until they're quiet.

Daniel admitted he had almost messaged her ten times but feared becoming annoying.

That's unfortunate, Lia wrote, because I also kept checking Messenger.

A laughing reaction appeared.

Thank you for not trying to fix me.

I don't think you need fixing. I think maybe you got tired.

Nobody said it like that before.

Everybody keeps asking what’s wrong. You asked if I was okay.

That night, Daniel asked: If somebody notices you... do you let them?

I don't know, Lia replied. But maybe I'm trying.

He reacted with a heart.

For the first time, the silence between them didn't feel empty.

It felt like someone finally stopped pretending.

sections.title: Chapter 14
sections.html:
Chapter 14

Don’t Log Out Yet

The next few days felt softer.

Not easier. Just softer.

Daniel still disappeared sometimes. Replies still came late. Conversations still ended unexpectedly.

But something had changed. Lia stopped treating silence like rejection. Daniel stopped pretending everything was fine.

One rainy evening in Hong Kong, a message arrived.

Bad day.

That was all.

Lia did not ask what happened. Instead, she typed: Do you want company or quiet?

That's a good question. I don't know.

Okay. Then I'll stay here until you figure it out.

After several minutes he wrote: Can I say something stupid?

Historically yes.

I almost disappeared again today. I typed goodbye messages in my head. Not forever. Just disappearing. Turning everything off.

Thank you for telling me instead.

I didn't want to become someone people remember as unavailable.

Lia looked at the rain on the glass and began typing more than usual.

You don't have to answer this. But I wanted to say something before I overthink and don't send it.

You once asked me if somebody notices you... do you let them. I don't know the answer.

But I think disappearing before people leave isn't protection. Sometimes it just means nobody gets the chance to stay.

And maybe not everybody leaves because they're tired of you. Maybe some people stay because they want to.

So if your day is heavy--okay. If your replies are slow--okay. If you need quiet--okay.

Just don't log out without letting somebody know.

Because somebody might notice.

She almost deleted it.

Then she sent it.

Ten minutes passed. Fifteen.

Then Daniel replied: I read that three times before replying.

Nobody ever says stay. People usually say get better. You said stay.

I think I needed to hear that.

Lia typed only: Okay.

Then Daniel asked: If I disappear again... will you tell me to come back?

I'll remind you the door isn't locked.

He reacted with a heart.

No more messages after that.

Just Active Now.

For a little longer than usual.

And for some reason, that felt like enough.

sections.title: Chapter 15
sections.html:
Chapter 15

Active Now

Lia expected less after that.

The message had been too honest. Too revealing. Too close to something she wasn't ready to name.

So the next morning, she made a decision.

No checking. No waiting. No opening Messenger first.

She reached for her phone. Opened Messenger. Immediately closed it.

Okay. That didn't count.

At lunch, she opened Messenger again. No new message, but under Daniel's profile picture was a small green circle.

Active Now.

It was ridiculous how much that tiny dot mattered.

She closed the app. Opened it again.

Still there.

Two minutes later, Daniel messaged: Caught you.

Excuse me?

You opened Messenger four times in three minutes.

That information feels illegal.

You were checking if I disappeared again.

Research purposes.

Sure. I'm okay today.

Her shoulders relaxed.

He sent that before she asked.

Then came his question of the day: If someone gave you one free day--no responsibilities--what would you do?

Sleep. Walk somewhere nice. Call my family. Maybe coffee.

You forgot something.

What?

You never include yourself.

I don't know what I'd do for myself.

That answer made me sad. Okay, new rule. Once a day you have to do one thing that isn't useful.

That sounds expensive.

No. Just unnecessary. Useful and alive aren't always the same thing.

That evening, Lia got off one station early, bought iced coffee, and sat by the water.

She sent a picture.

Being unnecessary.

Daniel replied with a Texas sunset and coffee.

Participation points?

Accepted.

Then he wrote: Last week I thought disappearing would feel easier. Today I sat outside because I wanted to send you this sunset.

I'm glad you stayed.

Me too.

Would it be weird if I said I look for your green dot now?

Good, Lia typed. Because I look for yours too.

A heart reaction appeared.

Then three words.

Active now.

Stay awhile, she replied.

And for the first time, that tiny green circle didn't feel like online status.

It felt like someone quietly saying, I'm here.

sections.title: Chapter 16
sections.html:
Chapter 16

Recovery

Recovery did not arrive dramatically.

Nobody woke up transformed. Nobody posted inspirational quotes. Nobody announced: I am healed.

Life was less cinematic than that.

Recovery looked smaller.

It looked like replying a little faster. Opening curtains. Eating lunch. Laughing before thinking. Making plans for next week. Noticing the weather again.

Two weeks passed.

Their conversations changed. Not less deep. Just lighter.

Daniel still had difficult days. Lia still came home exhausted. But now there were other things too.

Random things. Normal things.

Daniel sent a photo of coffee.

Today’s review: expensive and emotionally average.

Strong criticism.

Recovery means honesty.

Who said recovery?

Okay maybe not recovery. Maybe returning.

Returning sounds nicer.

Less pressure.

A few days later, Daniel posted on Facebook. Not a quote. Not a dark background. Just a picture of blue sky and coffee.

Nice weather today.

Lia reacted with a heart.

Messenger buzzed.

You noticed.

Weather content era.

Trying new genres.

I like this genre.

Me too.

That night, they talked about childhood summers, Texas rain, gas station snacks, Philippine power outages, neighbors borrowing ingredients, and sleeping with electric fans.

Then Daniel asked if people could become important unexpectedly.

I think most important people start unexpectedly, Lia answered.

Do you think people can help each other without fixing each other?

I think helping isn't always solving. Sometimes it's reminding somebody they still exist outside difficult days.

I think you did that.

You did too.

How?

You reminded me I'm more than useful.

That might be my favorite thing you ever said.

On Saturday, Daniel sent a photo from a park.

Outside voluntarily.

Question.

Retired from questions, Lia replied.

Impossible. What’s something you want to do someday?

Travel without counting money. And sit somewhere beautiful with no schedule.

Okay. Added to future list.

Future list?

Just... things people should get to do.

That night, Daniel sent one final message.

Today felt normal.

I'm glad.

Me too. I missed normal.

Lia placed her phone down and realized recovery wasn't becoming who you used to be.

Maybe it was becoming someone who wanted tomorrow again.


Bridge Chapter

Last Message

For a while, tomorrow returned.

Not perfectly.

Not forever.

But enough that Lia stopped counting silence by the hour.

Daniel sent coffee again.

She sent water views again.

They talked about ordinary things: weather, food, the price of flights neither of them bought, and whether instant coffee deserved respect.

Then one week, his messages slowed.

Not suddenly.

Not enough to panic.

Just enough to notice.

A good morning became a reply at night.

A question of the day became a heart reaction.

A photo became only Seen.

Lia remembered what he had said before: some people disappear slowly.

So she tried not to fear it.

She sent gentle messages.

No pressure. Just checking in.

I hope today is lighter.

The door is not locked.

Some became seen.

Some stayed delivered.

Then one night, after work, Lia opened Messenger and saw something that made her sit very still.

Last Seen 3 Days Ago.

No new message.

No active status.

No coffee photo.

Just that small line.

Three days.

Ate Grace called from across the room, asking if she wanted dinner.

Lia did not answer right away.

She stared at Daniel's name, at the quiet profile picture, at all the messages that had once made the distance feel smaller.

She typed:

Are you still there?

She did not send it.

Not yet.

Instead, she placed the phone beside her and looked out at Hong Kong.

The city kept glowing.

The buses kept moving.

The world did not pause for unread messages.

But Lia did.


Final Chapter

Last Seen Online

Lia was folding clothes in Hong Kong when her phone vibrated.

Facebook notification.

At first she ignored it.

Then she saw the name.

Daniel.

Her heart paused.

She opened Messenger.

No new message.

Only--

Last Seen 3 Days Ago

Strange.

She opened his profile.

Nothing.

No stories.

No updates.

No reactions.

Hours later, a message arrived.

Not from Daniel.

From his sister.

Hi. I don't know if Daniel talked about you... but I saw your messages.

Lia sat down.

Another message appeared.

He had been carrying things quietly for a long time.

Pause.

He talked about your conversations.

Pause.

You gave him moments he looked forward to.

Lia stared.

Her eyes blurred.

She kept reading.

Thank you for being kind to him.

Lia closed her eyes.

Not because she believed she should have known.

Not because she believed she could have solved everything.

But because she realized--

people can laugh.

Reply.

Show up.

And still carry things nobody can see.

Days later, she opened their chat.

Coffee pictures.

Good mornings.

Questions.

Ordinary conversations.

She typed one final message.

Not expecting anything.

Not needing anything.

Just words.

Thank you for showing up in my life.

Pause.

I hope wherever life became heavy, you also had moments that felt light.

Pause.

And thank you for staying as long as you could.

She looked at the message.

Then closed Messenger.

She never sent it.

Instead, she called her family.

Checked on friends.

Answered messages.

Started asking different questions.

Not--

How are you?

But--

How are you really doing?

Months later, she made a Facebook post.

No photos.

No filters.

Just words.

Be gentle with people. Some battles are invisible.

Thousands saw it.

Hundreds reacted.

One comment stood out.

Thank you. I needed this today.

Lia smiled.

And replied--

Stay awhile.

THE END

About the Author

Sunday Creative Studio creates beginner-friendly digital products, ebooks, prompts, and creative stories for modern readers and online creators. The goal is simple: make useful, emotional, and inspiring content that people can understand, enjoy, and share.

Thank You Note

Thank you for reading Last Seen Online. If this story reminded you of someone, send them a message. If you are the one quietly carrying something, may this book remind you that you matter. Stay awhile.
